messages.content: I want to design runtime verification for multicore embedded controllers. The central challenge is to preserve deadline guarantees and sound verdicts even though telemetry is asynchronous and may be lost.

That sets two constraints on the design at once. The monitor must interpret observations cautiously enough that asynchronous delivery or missing telemetry cannot make an unsupported verdict appear certain. It must also fit within the controllers’ timing constraints, so the act of monitoring does not cause a specified deadline to be missed.
The verdict requirement is more precise than simply handling missing data gracefully: verdicts must be sound under telemetry loss. How should I understand that?

A sound verdict is one justified by the information available despite possible loss. In particular, a missing telemetry report is not, by itself, proof that the reported event did not occur. If loss leaves both a compliant execution and a violating execution consistent with the observations, the monitor should not claim certainty about either one on that basis. This describes the required meaning of a verdict, not a particular mechanism for producing it.
Does soundness mean the monitor has to give a definitive answer for every execution, including when reports are lost?

No. Soundness concerns whether a verdict that is given is justified; it does not require a definitive verdict whenever telemetry is incomplete. An inconclusive outcome can be appropriate when the observations do not distinguish the possibilities. The requirement does not specify a particular set of verdict labels or require completeness under telemetry loss.
There is a separate completeness condition: when telemetry is lossless, monitoring must be complete for bounded-response violations.

Right. Under the lossless-telemetry condition, a bounded-response violation must not go undetected. Conceptually, a bounded-response obligation says that some required response must occur within its applicable bound after a triggering event. Completeness here concerns violations of that kind. It does not, as stated, extend the same guarantee to lossy telemetry or assert completeness for every possible class of property.
So I should keep the conditions attached to each claim: sound verdicts even with telemetry loss, but completeness for bounded-response violations when telemetry is lossless?

Exactly. Those claims have different scopes. Loss may limit what can be concluded, but it must not make an asserted verdict unsound. When telemetry is lossless, the monitor must also detect bounded-response violations. Neither condition should be silently weakened into a best-effort aspiration or broadened into a guarantee the requirement does not state.
What part does asynchronous telemetry play? Is it just another way of saying that reports can be missing?

They are distinct difficulties. Loss concerns reports that do not arrive; asynchrony concerns when reports arrive and how their arrival relates to the events they describe. For example, receiving one report before another need not, on its own, establish the order of the underlying events. A sound interpretation must avoid treating delivery order as stronger evidence than it is. No particular ordering or reconciliation technique is specified here.
For a bounded-response obligation, could a missing response report alone establish a violation?

Not if that report might have been lost and no other information rules out a timely response. Otherwise, an execution in which the response occurred but its telemetry was dropped could be labeled a violation. Under lossless telemetry, the completeness requirement is different: actual bounded-response violations must be detectable, rather than hidden by missing reports.
I also need a concrete timing constraint. Monitoring must add no more than 5% worst-case execution time per control job while preserving all specified deadlines.

That is a per-control-job worst-case overhead limit: monitoring adds ≤5% worst-case execution time per control job. It is not merely a limit on average overhead or an aggregate figure across jobs. Preserving all specified deadlines is an additional requirement; staying within the per-job overhead limit alone does not establish that every deadline remains satisfied.
Why separate the 5% limit from the deadline guarantee?

They ask different questions. The ≤5% condition bounds how much worst-case execution time monitoring adds to each control job. Deadline preservation asks whether the monitored multicore controller still meets every specified deadline. A bounded addition to each job’s execution time can still matter to timing, so both claims have to hold rather than one serving as a substitute for the other.
Does the goal say how the monitoring work must be divided among cores, or how telemetry is transported?

No. It specifies the setting—multicore embedded controllers with asynchronous, lossy telemetry—and the required outcomes, but not a core assignment, transport, or monitoring architecture. Those details cannot be treated as established parts of the design from this goal alone.

Then the design target is a monitor that makes only sound claims when telemetry can be lost, detects bounded-response violations when telemetry is lossless, adds ≤5% worst-case execution time per control job, and leaves every specified deadline intact.

Yes. That keeps the qualifications intact: sound verdicts despite asynchronous, lossy telemetry; completeness specifically for bounded-response violations under lossless telemetry; a ≤5% worst-case execution-time addition for each control job; and preservation of all specified deadlines in the multicore embedded controller.

For the runtime-verification design, I propose sequenced per-core logs, bounded-skew timestamps, gap-aware three-valued bounded-response monitors, and response-time-certified 5% instrumentation budgets.

Those components address different parts of the goal. Sequenced per-core logs give the monitor an order for observations from each core and a way to recognize some missing entries. Bounded-skew timestamps help it reason about timing across cores without assuming clocks agree exactly. A gap-aware three-valued monitor can distinguish a supported verdict from an inconclusive one when telemetry is incomplete. Response-time-certified instrumentation budgets address the ≤5% worst-case execution-time limit per control job and the requirement to preserve all specified deadlines. This is a proposed design, not yet a demonstrated set of guarantees.
Why make the logs per-core and sequenced rather than just process telemetry in the order it arrives?

Arrival order can reflect asynchronous delivery rather than the order of events being monitored. A sequence within each core’s log provides an order that does not depend on when those entries reach the monitor. It can also reveal a gap if an observed sequence skips an entry. The proposal does not, by itself, establish a total order between events on different cores.
Does seeing a sequence gap tell the monitor what happened in the missing entry?

No. A gap indicates that the monitor lacks at least part of the relevant log sequence; it does not reveal the missing entry’s contents. For a bounded-response check, a missing entry might contain an event that changes the verdict. Gap awareness means taking that possibility into account rather than treating the absent entry as evidence that the event did not occur.
And a log with no visible gap is not necessarily proof that nothing was lost?

Correct. Sequencing makes certain gaps recognizable when surrounding sequence information is observed. The mere absence of a visible gap does not, on its own, justify assuming a complete record. The proposal’s soundness requirement still governs what the monitor may conclude from what it has actually received.
What does bounded skew contribute if each core already has its own sequence?

Per-core sequences address ordering within a core’s log. Bounded-skew timestamps address timing comparisons involving different cores, which matter when an obligation can be triggered on one core and answered on another. A bound on clock skew lets the monitor account for uncertainty in such comparisons. It must not treat timestamps as perfectly synchronized merely because each entry has one.
So if the timestamp uncertainty makes it unclear whether a response occurred within a bound, the monitor should not guess?

Yes. If the observations and allowed timing uncertainty admit both an in-bound and an out-of-bound interpretation, a definite verdict would need further justification. The bounded-skew condition is meant to support sound time reasoning, not to erase ambiguity that the bound leaves unresolved. No numerical skew bound or particular timestamp-processing rule is specified in this proposal.
Explain the three values in the bounded-response monitor without assuming a particular implementation.

Conceptually, they are satisfied, violated, and inconclusive. A satisfied verdict needs sufficient evidence that the bounded-response obligation was met; a violated verdict needs sufficient evidence that it was not. Inconclusive covers cases where missing log entries, asynchronous observations, or timing uncertainty prevent either definitive conclusion. Those labels describe the intended distinction, not a prescribed internal representation.
How is that monitor specifically gap-aware rather than merely three-valued?

It considers gaps when deciding which verdicts the observed telemetry supports. For example, if a response could have been recorded in a missing portion of a log, the monitor cannot infer a violation solely from not seeing that response. Likewise, it should not assume that an unobserved trigger never occurred if a gap could contain it. The third value gives it a way to express that uncertainty instead of turning incomplete telemetry into a false certainty.
Would three-valued monitoring under loss conflict with completeness for bounded-response violations?

Not as the requirements are stated. Soundness applies under telemetry loss, where an inconclusive result may be necessary. Completeness for bounded-response violations applies when telemetry is lossless: in that condition, an actual violation must be detected. The proposal has to support both claims under their respective conditions; the presence of an inconclusive value is not permission to leave lossless bounded-response violations undetected.
Can the combination of sequences and bounded-skew timestamps alone establish that completeness guarantee?

The combination is a proposed basis for interpreting the event order and timing, but the guarantee would still need to be established for the bounded-response monitor. In particular, one would have to show that, when telemetry is lossless, every bounded-response violation receives a violation verdict while the treatment of asynchronous arrival and clock skew remains sound. The proposal names the components; it does not claim that proof has already been completed.
I do not want the timing part reduced to saying that 5% overhead sounds small. What does a response-time-certified instrumentation budget require in principle?

It requires the monitoring overhead to be accounted for against the controller’s worst-case timing obligations, not merely estimated by average behavior. The proposed budget limits added worst-case execution time to ≤5% for each control job. Response-time certification must also establish that, with monitoring included, all specified deadlines remain satisfied. The per-job percentage and the deadline result are separate conditions, both of which the proposed approach is meant to meet.
Does a 5% budget let one control job exceed its limit if another uses less?

No. The stated limit is per control job: monitoring adds no more than 5% of that job’s worst-case execution time. Spare capacity attributed to a different job does not, by itself, change that individual limit. Nor does meeting the limit dispense with checking deadline preservation.
Should I describe these elements as a completed solution or as a design proposal that still needs its verdict and timing guarantees justified?

As a design proposal. It identifies how to approach asynchronous, lossy telemetry and the controller’s timing constraints: sequenced per-core logs, bounded-skew timestamps, gap-aware three-valued bounded-response monitors, and response-time-certified 5% instrumentation budgets. Its intended guarantees are sound verdicts under telemetry loss, completeness for bounded-response violations when telemetry is lossless, ≤5% added worst-case execution time per control job, and preservation of all specified deadlines. Naming the approach does not itself certify those properties.
What heartbeat period, delivery bound, and clock-skew limit would permit sound violation finalization after a response deadline?

There is no numerical answer in the requirements so far. More importantly, finite heartbeat, delivery, and skew bounds alone do not necessarily justify a violation verdict under telemetry loss. To finalize a violation, the monitor must know not just that the response deadline has passed, but that a timely response could not be hidden in missing or still-in-flight telemetry. We would need to specify what a heartbeat establishes, what the delivery bound covers, and how timestamp uncertainty is bounded before choosing values.
Could the monitor simply wait one heartbeat period after the response deadline, then declare a violation if no response report has arrived?

Not on that basis alone. A response might have occurred on time while its report was lost. A heartbeat arriving later would resolve that uncertainty only if it supplied trustworthy evidence about the completeness of the relevant event record. If it merely says that a core is active, it does not prove that no response occurred.
Then is the key distinction whether a heartbeat attests to log coverage rather than just liveness?

Yes. Liveness and coverage support different conclusions. A liveness heartbeat can indicate that communication is occurring, but it cannot by itself rule out a missing response entry. A heartbeat that reliably establishes which portion of a sequenced per-core log has been completely accounted for could help the monitor reason about absence. Whether heartbeats have that meaning is not specified yet, so it must be treated as a condition to define, not an existing guarantee.
How would the delivery bound matter if reports can still be lost?

A bound on delivery time can limit how long a report that will be delivered might remain in flight. It does not imply that a lost report will eventually arrive. Thus, waiting past a delivery bound can address delayed telemetry only under the bound’s stated assumptions; it cannot convert possible loss into evidence that the event never happened. If the relevant log coverage remains uncertain, the gap-aware monitor should remain inconclusive rather than finalize a violation.
Could I express the question using a symbolic heartbeat period H, delivery bound D, and clock-skew limit ε without choosing numbers yet?

Certainly. H, D, and ε can name the quantities whose limits need to be established. H affects when the next relevant heartbeat could provide information; D affects when information covered by an applicable delivery guarantee should have arrived; and ε limits uncertainty when comparing timestamps across cores. But a finalization rule cannot be derived from those symbols alone. It also needs the precise meaning of heartbeat coverage, the scope of the delivery guarantee, and the timing interpretation of the response deadline.
Why does clock skew affect the point at which the response deadline is safely past?

If a trigger and response are timestamped using clocks on different cores, their timestamps cannot necessarily be compared as though they came from one perfectly synchronized clock. A bounded skew permits a sound comparison only while accounting for its uncertainty. Before declaring a violation, the monitor has to allow for a response that may still count as timely under every timing interpretation consistent with the stated skew limit. The exact allowance depends on how the timestamps and skew bound are defined.
Would a smaller ε solve the telemetry-loss problem?

No. A smaller skew limit narrows timing uncertainty; it does not reveal a response report that may have been lost. Likewise, a shorter heartbeat period can make relevant information available sooner only if those heartbeats actually convey the needed coverage evidence. The timing and loss questions both have to be resolved for a sound final violation verdict.
Suppose a per-core log has a sequence gap covering the relevant interval. Can the monitor finalize a violation once D has elapsed?

Not merely because D elapsed. If the missing sequence entry could contain a timely response, a delivery-time bound does not tell the monitor its contents. Unless some additional trustworthy evidence resolves that gap, a violation verdict would not be sound. Waiting longer and learning what happened are different things.
What if there is no observed gap?

That is useful, but absence of an observed gap must not automatically be equated with proof of complete telemetry. The monitor needs a justified way to know that the relevant log interval has been accounted for. For example, the meaning assigned to sequence progress or heartbeat coverage might provide that assurance, but it is not established just by selecting H, D, and ε.
Is there at least a qualitative rule for when finalization becomes possible?

Yes: finalize a bounded-response violation only when the response deadline is certainly past under the applicable clock uncertainty, all telemetry that could establish a timely response has either been received or is covered by trustworthy evidence of its absence, and no unresolved gap could change the conclusion. A heartbeat period and delivery bound can affect when those conditions become knowable, but they are not substitutes for the conditions themselves.
How does this question relate to completeness when telemetry is lossless?

In the lossless case, a bounded-response violation must ultimately receive a violation verdict. To establish a finite point for that verdict after the response deadline, the design would also need suitable bounds on when the relevant observations or coverage evidence become available, together with a sound treatment of clock skew. The stated completeness requirement does not supply numerical values for H, D, or ε, or specify a finalization-latency bound.
And under lossy telemetry, it is acceptable for the monitor to stay inconclusive if it cannot exclude an unobserved timely response?

Yes. Sound verdicts under telemetry loss do not require definitive verdicts from incomplete evidence. If a possible lost report could change whether the bounded-response obligation was met, inconclusive is the cautious outcome. A definitive violation becomes appropriate only when the available evidence, including any warranted coverage guarantees, rules that possibility out.
Do the heartbeat choices also have to respect the controller’s execution-time and deadline constraints?

They do if heartbeat generation or related instrumentation adds work to control jobs. The monitoring design still has to keep added worst-case execution time at ≤5% per control job and preserve every specified deadline. A heartbeat period cannot be chosen solely for prompt verdicts while ignoring those timing requirements. No feasible period or response-time certification has been established here.

So the open question is not just to find three small numbers. It is to determine, under explicit coverage and timing assumptions, whether particular bounds let the monitor safely close the response interval and issue a violation verdict.

Exactly. The heartbeat period, delivery bound, and clock-skew limit need to be evaluated together with what heartbeats prove about sequenced logs and what loss can leave unknown. Until those meanings and bounds are specified, there is no justified numerical finalization threshold after a response deadline.

I have a hypothesis for the finalization question: with 2 ms heartbeats, 1 ms delivery, and 100 µs skew, contiguous per-core watermarks soundly finalize bounded-response violations within 3.2 ms after the response deadline.

That is a concrete hypothesis, not yet an established guarantee. It proposes that those heartbeat, delivery, and skew bounds, together with contiguous per-core watermarks, are sufficient both for a sound violation verdict and for a finalization delay of at most 3.2 ms after the response deadline. The important qualification is what a watermark certifies: the monitor must be able to rule out a timely response hidden in missing or still-in-flight telemetry.
What should “contiguous” contribute to that claim?

It should mean that the portion of each relevant per-core log covered by its watermark has no unresolved sequence gap. A watermark that merely identifies the highest sequence number seen would not, by itself, establish that all earlier entries were accounted for. Contiguity matters because an unresolved entry could contain the response whose absence the monitor is trying to establish.
Is a contiguous watermark enough by itself to declare the violation?

Only if its coverage has the necessary meaning. The monitor would need to know that the watermarks cover all relevant places and times where a timely response could appear, and that a logged response would not be silently omitted from a supposedly complete interval. It must also account for the 100 µs clock-skew limit when deciding where that interval ends. Those are conditions the hypothesis needs to justify, rather than consequences of the word “contiguous” alone.
I still want the claim to hold despite lossy telemetry. Does a lost heartbeat invalidate the soundness part?

A lost heartbeat need not force an unsound verdict; it may instead prevent a definitive verdict until adequate coverage evidence arrives. The distinction is between soundness and the proposed 3.2 ms finalization bound. If loss can withhold the watermark needed to rule out a timely response, the monitor should remain inconclusive. The timing claim therefore needs a clear condition under which the requisite contiguous watermarks are available within that bound.
So I should not say that 2 ms heartbeats alone guarantee a violation verdict within 3.2 ms even if any number of heartbeats are lost?

Correct. A 2 ms heartbeat period describes when heartbeats are generated or expected under the proposed arrangement; it does not make a lost heartbeat arrive. If the evidence needed for finalization can be lost without replacement within the stated interval, an unconditional 3.2 ms verdict guarantee would require some further justification. Soundness must take priority over finalizing on time when the evidence is insufficient.
How does the 1 ms delivery bound enter the hypothesis?

It is a proposed limit on delivery delay for telemetry to which that guarantee applies. Together with the 2 ms heartbeat period, it could help bound when a qualifying watermark becomes available. But a delivery bound does not establish the contents of a lost report, and its exact scope matters: the 3.2 ms argument needs the relevant coverage evidence to be delivered under the assumed bound. That argument has not yet been shown.
Is the 100 µs skew simply another 100 µs added to the waiting time?

Not necessarily. The proposal specifies a 100 µs clock-skew limit, but it does not specify the clock model or the derivation of the 3.2 ms figure. Skew must be accounted for when deciding whether a response could have occurred before the deadline across cores. We should not infer a particular arithmetic rule for the skew allowance without defining the timestamp comparisons it supports.
Numerically, 2 ms plus 1 ms is 3 ms, leaving 0.2 ms in the proposed 3.2 ms. Can I call that the clock-skew allowance?

You can observe that 3.2 ms exceeds 2 ms plus 1 ms by 0.2 ms, or 200 µs. But assigning that entire difference to clock skew—and showing that it is sufficient—requires an argument about how the 100 µs skew bound applies to the relevant timestamps. The arithmetic alone does not prove sound finalization or the claimed latency.
Does the monitor need a watermark from every core in the controller?

It needs coverage sufficient to rule out every timely response relevant to the particular obligation. If a response could be represented in more than one per-core log, relying on only one log’s watermark could leave an unexcluded possibility. The hypothesis says “contiguous per-core watermarks” but does not specify which cores are relevant to each obligation, so that scope must be made explicit before claiming a proof.
What if a watermark has arrived, but one of the covered logs still has a gap?

Then it is not contiguous over that gap in the sense needed for the claim. If the missing entry could affect whether a timely response occurred, the monitor cannot soundly finalize a violation on the strength of that watermark. A later, genuinely complete coverage indication might resolve the uncertainty, but the present hypothesis cannot treat a gap as proof of absence.
Would the same hypothesis mean every actual bounded-response violation is reported within 3.2 ms when telemetry is lossless?

That would be a natural consequence to seek, but it is still a claim to establish. In the lossless case, the required log entries and watermarks would need to arrive with the proposed timing and cover the response interval, while the monitor’s rule would need to recognize each actual bounded-response violation. The stated hypothesis names a 3.2 ms finalization bound; it does not supply a proof that all those conditions hold.
I want to keep the verdict meaning precise: does “finalize a violation” mean that no later telemetry can turn that verdict into a satisfied one?

For a sound finalized verdict, yes: later telemetry consistent with the stated guarantees must not reveal a timely response that the monitor had overlooked. That is why the watermark must establish adequate contiguous coverage, rather than just indicate that some recent heartbeat arrived. If later admissible telemetry could overturn the verdict, the earlier finalization was premature.
Does this hypothesis also settle the monitoring overhead and deadline requirements?

No. The 2 ms heartbeat period, 1 ms delivery bound, 100 µs skew limit, and 3.2 ms verdict-finalization claim concern telemetry and verdict timing. The design separately requires monitoring to add ≤5% worst-case execution time per control job and to preserve all specified deadlines. This hypothesis does not state that response-time certification or the per-job overhead check has been completed.

Then I should present 3.2 ms as the proposed bound after the response deadline, conditional on proving that the contiguous per-core watermarks establish complete relevant coverage under those timing assumptions.

Yes. The hypothesis is that 2 ms heartbeats, 1 ms delivery, and 100 µs skew permit contiguous per-core watermarks to support sound violation finalization within 3.2 ms after a response deadline. Its validity depends on a precise watermark-coverage and clock-timing argument, especially when telemetry can be lost. Until that argument is established, 3.2 ms is a proposed bound, not a certified result.
I want to turn the finalization hypothesis into a plan: derive watermark closure bounds, then simulate packet loss and clock skew to check unknown verdicts and 3.2 ms lossless finalization.

That separates the work into a timing argument and a behavioral check. The derivation would establish when contiguous per-core watermarks can close the relevant response interval. The simulations would examine whether packet loss leads to an unknown verdict when the missing information matters, and whether violations are finalized within 3.2 ms after the response deadline when telemetry is lossless. These are planned checks, not results.
What exactly should the watermark closure bound describe?

It should bound when the monitor has sufficient evidence that the interval in which a timely response could have occurred is completely covered. That is more specific than bounding when a heartbeat arrives. Closure requires both that the deadline is certainly past under the clock-skew assumption and that the relevant per-core log coverage has no unresolved gap that could conceal a timely response.
Would deriving the bound mean just adding the heartbeat period and delivery bound?

No. Those bounds may contribute to when coverage information becomes available, but their sum alone does not establish what a watermark covers or how clock skew affects the deadline comparison. The derivation needs to state the assumptions under which a contiguous watermark rules out a still-unseen timely response. It should distinguish waiting for evidence from having evidence that the response did not occur.
Should the derivation explicitly separate the deadline from the time at which the monitor can finalize?

Yes. The response deadline marks the end of the obligation’s allowed response interval. Finalization is a later monitoring action that depends on when sound coverage evidence becomes available. The proposed 3.2 ms figure is a bound on that delay after the response deadline in the lossless case, not a change to the response deadline itself.
How does the existing 2 ms heartbeat, 1 ms delivery, and 100 µs skew hypothesis fit into this plan?

Those are the proposed timing parameters whose implications the closure derivation would examine. It would need to show how a 2 ms heartbeat period and 1 ms delivery bound make the requisite watermark available, and how the 100 µs clock-skew limit affects safe closure. The plan should not assume that the parameters imply 3.2 ms merely because they were proposed together.
What should I be looking for in the packet-loss simulation?

The central check is whether uncertainty caused by lost telemetry is represented as an unknown verdict rather than a definitive violation or satisfaction that the available evidence cannot support. In particular, if lost information could contain a timely response, the monitor should not finalize a violation solely because the response report was not observed. The simulation can examine that behavior, but it cannot by itself prove soundness for every possible loss pattern.
Does an unknown verdict mean the monitor failed?

Not necessarily. Under telemetry loss, unknown can be the sound result when the observations leave both compliance and violation possible. What would be concerning is a definitive verdict that depends on treating a possible lost report as though its contents were known. The plan is to check that distinction, not to eliminate unknown verdicts under all loss conditions.
What role should skew play in the simulation, apart from being a number in the derivation?

The skew check should examine whether verdicts respect the allowed uncertainty when timestamps from different cores are compared. If that uncertainty leaves a response possibly within its deadline, a definitive violation would need other justification. The derivation states the intended closure rule; simulation can probe whether the monitor behaves consistently with it under skew.
Can the loss and skew checks be combined conceptually?

Yes. They affect different sources of uncertainty that can coexist: loss can hide an event, and skew can make the timing of observed events ambiguous. The monitor should issue a definitive verdict only when neither uncertainty leaves a contrary execution consistent with the evidence. Combining them in a check does not change the separate need to justify watermark coverage and timing bounds.
For the 3.2 ms check, should I count runs with packet loss as failures if finalization takes longer?

The plan states a 3.2 ms check for lossless finalization. It should not silently extend that latency claim to runs where loss withholds the evidence needed for a sound verdict. Lossy runs serve the separate check of whether unknown verdicts are handled soundly. Keeping those conditions distinct makes the outcome of each check interpretable.
Does lossless finalization just mean that some verdict appears by 3.2 ms?

No. For an actual bounded-response violation, the relevant check is that a justified, finalized violation verdict appears within 3.2 ms after the response deadline when telemetry is lossless. An unknown verdict at that point would not establish the proposed finalization bound, and a premature violation verdict would not establish soundness merely because it arrived on time.
What if the simulation shows the intended behavior in every run I examine?

That would be evidence about the examined runs, not a general proof. The closure derivation would still need to support the timing claim under its stated assumptions, and soundness would still require an argument that a finalized verdict cannot be overturned by telemetry consistent with those assumptions. The plan appropriately includes both derivation and simulation rather than treating observed behavior alone as certification.
Should the watermark derivation cover only the core that reported the trigger?

It should cover whichever per-core logs could contain a response relevant to that obligation. Otherwise, closing one log could leave open the possibility of a timely response recorded elsewhere. The plan does not specify which cores those are, so the derivation would have to make the relevant coverage scope explicit without assuming that the trigger’s core is always sufficient.
And if a watermark advances while there is still a sequence gap?

Advancement alone would not close the gap. The derivation must rely on contiguous coverage of the relevant interval, not merely a high watermark value. In the simulation, an unresolved gap that could hide a timely response should lead to unknown rather than a finalized violation.
Is this plan also a way of certifying the ≤5% per-control-job instrumentation budget and every specified deadline?

No. Deriving watermark closure bounds and simulating loss and skew target verdict soundness and finalization timing. The separate requirements remain ≤5% added worst-case execution time per control job and preservation of all specified deadlines. This plan does not say that response-time certification or the instrumentation-budget check has been performed.

Then the immediate aim is to derive when the relevant watermarks safely close the response interval, and use simulations to check unknown verdicts under packet loss and skew and finalized violations within 3.2 ms after the deadline when telemetry is lossless.

Yes. That expresses the plan without turning it into an experimental result: derive the watermark closure bounds, simulate packet loss and clock skew to examine when verdicts remain unknown, and check the proposed 3.2 ms lossless violation-finalization bound. The closure argument and the checks must preserve the distinction between a verdict that is prompt and one that is sound.
The activity is to simulate four-core WatermarkBench with 2 ms heartbeats, 1 ms delivery, 100 µs clock skew, and injected loss, then check soundness and watermark closure.

That gives the evaluation a defined setting and timing assumptions. WatermarkBench has four cores; the simulation uses a 2 ms heartbeat period, a 1 ms delivery bound, and a 100 µs skew limit, with loss injected into telemetry. The checks concern whether verdicts remain sound despite that loss and whether watermarks close a response interval only when the evidence warrants closure. The activity does not itself report an outcome.
What should “check soundness” mean for the injected-loss cases?

It means examining whether a definitive verdict is supported by the observations despite possible missing telemetry. In particular, if a lost entry could contain a timely response, absence of an observed response cannot alone justify a finalized violation. The monitor should leave that case unknown unless other trustworthy coverage evidence excludes the response.
Would seeing an unknown verdict in WatermarkBench count as a problem?

Not necessarily. With injected loss, unknown may be exactly the sound verdict if the lost information could change the answer. The relevant distinction is between justified uncertainty and an unjustified definitive claim. This activity checks that behavior; it does not presume how the simulation will turn out.
How should I read the 1 ms delivery bound alongside injected loss?

Delivery time and loss are separate. A 1 ms delivery bound can constrain the arrival time of telemetry to which that bound applies, but it does not reveal the contents of a lost report. Thus, elapsed delivery time alone cannot close a gap that might conceal a timely response. The simulation needs to keep that distinction visible when checking verdicts.
And the 2 ms heartbeats are relevant to closure because they may advance the watermarks?

They may provide opportunities for watermark information to become available, depending on what the heartbeats establish. A 2 ms period does not, by itself, prove that the relevant log interval is complete, particularly when telemetry is lost. Closure depends on the meaning and continuity of the per-core watermarks, not simply on the arrival of a heartbeat.
What is the specific closure error to watch for?

Premature closure: treating a response interval as fully accounted for while a relevant per-core log still has an unresolved gap, a relevant report may still arrive within the delivery assumption, or the 100 µs skew uncertainty leaves a timely response possible. In any such case, a finalized violation would need evidence that resolves the uncertainty rather than an assumption that nothing happened.
Does “four-core” mean all four watermarks must always advance before every verdict?

Not necessarily. The soundness question is whether the watermarks cover every core on which a response relevant to the particular obligation could be recorded. The activity specifies four cores in WatermarkBench, but not which cores are relevant to each obligation. It would be unwarranted to assume either that one core always suffices or that all four are always needed.
Where does the 100 µs skew limit matter in this check?

It matters when event times from different cores are compared with the response deadline. A closure decision must allow for the timing uncertainty permitted by the 100 µs skew limit. If that uncertainty leaves an interpretation in which a response was timely, the monitor cannot finalize a violation merely by comparing timestamp values as if the clocks were identical.
The earlier hypothesis proposed finalizing within 3.2 ms after the response deadline. Does this injected-loss activity establish that timing claim?

Not merely by running injected-loss cases. Loss can withhold the coverage evidence required for a sound verdict, so those cases primarily probe whether the monitor remains appropriately unknown rather than finalizing prematurely. Checking the proposed 3.2 ms bound for lossless finalization requires observations under the lossless condition as well as a justified closure bound. The activity names soundness and closure checks but states no measured finalization time.
So if a response report is lost and a watermark appears to pass the deadline, what should the check ask?

It should ask whether that watermark truly certifies contiguous coverage of the relevant log interval, including the part in which the response could have been recorded. If the missing report leaves a gap, apparent progress past the deadline does not rule out a timely response.
